claim: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are ~22-nt regulatory RNAs that are processed from hairpin precursors.
source: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are ~22-nt regulatory RNAs that are processed from hairpin precursors.
evidence: This is established knowledge about miRNA biogenesis and structure, supported by citations in the manuscript.

claim: Upon processing, miRNAs associate with an Argonaute (AGO) protein and base-pair to sites within mRNAs to direct the destabilization and/or translational repression of these mRNA targets.
source: Upon processing, miRNAs associate with an Argonaute (AGO) protein and base-pair to sites within mRNAs to direct the destabilization and/or translational repression of these mRNA targets (Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015; Bartel, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Jonas and Izaurralde, 2015 and Bartel, 2018.

claim: For most sites that confer repression in mammalian cells, pairing to miRNA nucleotides 2–7, referred to as the miRNA seed, is critical for target recognition.
source: For most sites that confer repression in mammalian cells, pairing to miRNA nucleotides 2–7, referred to as the miRNA seed, is critical for target recognition, with an additional pair to miRNA position 8 or an A across from miRNA position 1 often enhancing targeting efficacy (Lewis et al., 2005; Bartel, 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Lewis et al., 2005 and Bartel, 2009.

claim: Sites with a perfect 6–8-nucleotide match to the miRNA seed region are heuristically predictive of repression, with longer sites being more effective than shorter ones and more sites being more effective than fewer sites.
source: Such sites with a perfect 6–8-nucleotide (nt) match to the miRNA seed region (Figure 1A, left) are heuristically predictive of repression, with longer sites being more effective than shorter ones and more sites being more effective than fewer sites (Grimson et al., 2007; Agarwal et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grimson et al., 2007 and Agarwal et al., 2015.

claim: Contextual features extrinsic to a site itself can influence targeting efficacy.
source: In addition, contextual features extrinsic to a site itself can influence targeting efficacy (Brown et al., 2005; Ameres et al., 2007; Grimson et al., 2007; Kedde et al., 2007; Nielsen et al., 2007; Saetrom et al., 2007; Tafer et al., 2008; Kedde et al., 2010; Wan et al., 2014; Agarwal et al., 2015; McGeary et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Pairing to the miRNA 3′ region, particularly pairing that includes miRNA nucleotides 13–16, can supplement perfect seed pairing to enhance targeting efficacy beyond that of seed pairing alone.
source: Pairing to the miRNA 3′ region, particularly pairing that includes miRNA nucleotides 13–16, can supplement perfect seed pairing to enhance targeting efficacy beyond that of seed pairing alone, and extensive pairing to the 3′ region can compensate for imperfect seed pairing to enable consequential repression (Brennecke et al., 2005; Lewis et al., 2005; Grimson et al., 2007).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Brennecke et al., 2005, Lewis et al., 2005, and Grimson et al., 2007.

claim: 3′-supplementary sites comprise ~5% of all conserved sites observed in mammals.
source: Although 3′-supplementary sites are less common than sites with only a seed match, comprising ~5% of all conserved sites observed in mammals, thousands of sites with preferentially conserved 3′-supplementary pairing are present in human 3′ UTRs (Grimson et al., 2007; Friedman et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Grimson et al., 2007 and Friedman et al., 2009.

claim: Conserved 3′-compensatory sites comprise only ~1.5% of all preferentially conserved sites observed in human 3′ UTRs.
source: Conserved 3′-compensatory sites are even less common, comprising only ~1.5% of all preferentially conserved sites observed in human 3′ UTRs (Friedman et al., 2009).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Friedman et al., 2009.

claim: Two instances of 3′-compensatory sites within the 3′ UTR of lin-41 mediate the extreme morphological and developmental defects by which the let-7 miRNA was discovered in C. elegans.
source: Nonetheless, two instances of this relatively rare site type within the 3′ UTR of lin-41 mediate the extreme morphological and developmental defects by which the let-7 miRNA was discovered in C. elegans (Pasquinelli et al., 2000; Reinhart et al., 2000; Ecsedi et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Pasquinelli et al., 2000, Reinhart et al., 2000, and Ecsedi et al., 2015.

claim: Site mutations that create perfect seed pairing while maintaining the 3′ pairing cause precocious repression of the lin-41 mRNA by other members of the let-7 seed family expressed during earlier larval stages.
source: Moreover, the use of these 3′-compensatory sites rather than canonical sites for lin-41 repression is consequential; site mutations that create perfect seed pairing while maintaining the 3′ pairing cause precocious repression of the mRNA by other members of the let-7 seed family expressed during earlier larval stages (Brancati and Großhans, 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Brancati and Großhans, 2018.

claim: Pairing to positions 13–16 of let-7a imparts only a twofold increase in binding affinity.
source: Early measurements showed that pairing to positions 13–16 of let-7a imparts only a twofold increase in binding affinity, which led to the view that 3′-supplemental pairing contributes only modestly to affinity (Wee et al., 2012).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Wee et al., 2012.

claim: Pairing to positions 13–16 of miR-21 increases affinity by 11-fold.
source: Further measurements revealed some differences between miRNAs, with the observation that pairing to positions 13–16 of miR-21 increases affinity by 11-fold (Salomon et al., 2015), and a striking effect of longer pairing, with the observations that 10 bp of 3′-supplementary pairing to miR-122 and 9 bp of 3′-supplementary pairing (including a terminal G:U wobble) to miR-27a increases affinity by 20- and >400-fold, respectively (Sheu-Gruttadauria et al., 2019a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Salomon et al., 2015.

claim: 10 bp of 3′-supplementary pairing to miR-122 increases affinity by 20-fold.
source: Further measurements revealed some differences between miRNAs, with the observation that pairing to positions 13–16 of miR-21 increases affinity by 11-fold (Salomon et al., 2015), and a striking effect of longer pairing, with the observations that 10 bp of 3′-supplementary pairing to miR-122 and 9 bp of 3′-supplementary pairing (including a terminal G:U wobble) to miR-27a increases affinity by 20- and >400-fold, respectively (Sheu-Gruttadauria et al., 2019a).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sheu-Gruttadauria et al., 2019a.

claim: Binding affinity varies ~10-fold as the length of the target segment bridging the seed and 3′ pairing is varied over a range of 1–15 nt.
source: Other measurements illustrate the influence of the length of the target segment bridging the seed and 3′ pairing, with binding affinity varying ~10-fold as this length is varied over a range of 1–15 nt (Sheu-Gruttadauria et al., 2019b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sheu-Gruttadauria et al., 2019b.

claim: Imaging-based, high-throughput single-molecule biochemistry has been applied to acquire affinity measurements for ~23,000 sites for each of two miRNAs (let-7a and miR-21).
source: Imaging-based, high-throughput single-molecule biochemistry has recently been applied to acquire affinity measurements for ~23,000 sites for each of two miRNAs (let-7a and miR-21), including many sites with 3′ pairing (Becker et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Becker et al., 2019.

claim: miR-21 relies more on 3′ pairing when binding to a fully complementary target than does let-7a.
source: These measurements revealed that miR-21 relies more on 3′ pairing when binding to a fully complementary target than does let-7a, that homopolymeric insertions are the least disruptive to binding when inserted between nucleotides 8 and 11 within the context of fully complementary binding, and that mismatches near the miRNA 3′ terminus (after position 16) decrease binding affinity but increase target slicing.
evidence: This statement is based on data from Becker et al., 2019.

claim: Homopolymeric insertions are the least disruptive to binding when inserted between nucleotides 8 and 11 within the context of fully complementary binding.
source: These measurements revealed that miR-21 relies more on 3′ pairing when binding to a fully complementary target than does let-7a, that homopolymeric insertions are the least disruptive to binding when inserted between nucleotides 8 and 11 within the context of fully complementary binding, and that mismatches near the miRNA 3′ terminus (after position 16) decrease binding affinity but increase target slicing.
evidence: This statement is based on data from Becker et al., 2019.

claim: Mismatches near the miRNA 3′ terminus (after position 16) decrease binding affinity but increase target slicing.
source: These measurements revealed that miR-21 relies more on 3′ pairing when binding to a fully complementary target than does let-7a, that homopolymeric insertions are the least disruptive to binding when inserted between nucleotides 8 and 11 within the context of fully complementary binding, and that mismatches near the miRNA 3′ terminus (after position 16) decrease binding affinity but increase target slicing.
evidence: This statement is based on data from Becker et al., 2019.

claim: miRNA targeting efficacy observed in the cell is largely a function of the affinity between AGO–miRNA complexes and their sites.
source: The observation that miRNA targeting efficacy observed in the cell is largely a function of the affinity between AGO–miRNA complexes and their sites (McGeary et al., 2019) indicates that contributions of 3′ pairing to affinities measured in vitro can provide insight into biological targeting efficacy.
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to McGeary et al., 2019.

claim: The authors used RNA bind-n-seq with purified AGO2–miRNA complexes to measure relative affinities of >1000 3′-pairing architectures for each miRNA.
source: We used RNA bind-n-seq with purified AGO2–miRNA complexes to measure relative affinities of >1000 3′-pairing architectures for each miRNA.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental approach used in the study.

claim: In some cases, optimal 3′ pairing increased affinity by >500 fold.
source: In some cases, optimal 3′ pairing increased affinity by >500 fold.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study's data.

claim: Some miRNAs had two high-affinity 3′-pairing modes—one of which included additional nucleotides bridging seed and 3′ pairing to enable high-affinity pairing to miRNA nucleotide 11.
source: Some miRNAs had two high-affinity 3′-pairing modes—one of which included additional nucleotides bridging seed and 3′ pairing to enable high-affinity pairing to miRNA nucleotide 11.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study's data.

claim: The affinity of binding and the position of optimal pairing both tracked with the occurrence of G or oligo(G/C) nucleotides within the miRNA.
source: The affinity of binding and the position of optimal pairing both tracked with the occurrence of G or oligo(G/C) nucleotides within the miRNA.
evidence: This is a direct statement of a key finding from the study's data.

claim: The most enriched 8-nt k-mer was AUACAACC—the perfect Watson–Crick match to positions 11–18 of let-7a.
source: The most enriched was AUACAACC—the perfect Watson–Crick match to positions 11–18 of let-7a (Figure 1D).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The AUACAACC 8-nt 3′ site was most strongly enriched when starting at position 15 of the library, which suggested that an internal loop with two miRNA nucleotides (9 and 10) and six target-site nucleotides (positions 9–14) separating seed pairing and 3′ pairing was optimal.
source: This 8-nt 3′ site was most strongly enriched when starting at position 15 of the library, which suggested that an internal loop with two miRNA nucleotides (9 and 10) and six target-site nucleotides (positions 9–14) separating seed pairing and 3′ pairing was optimal (Figure 1D, top).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 1D and represents an inference from the enrichment pattern.

claim: The 8-nt, position-11 site was also ≥5-fold enriched at seven other neighboring offsets (corresponding to library positions 8–15), indicating that looping out 3–10 unpaired library nucleotides opposite miRNA nucleotides 9 and 10 was tolerated, albeit to varying degrees.
source: This 8-nt, position-11 site was also ≥5-fold enriched at seven other neighboring offsets (corresponding to library positions 8–15), indicating that looping out 3–10 unpaired library nucleotides opposite miRNA nucleotides 9 and 10 was tolerated, albeit to varying degrees (Figure 1D).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Perfect pairing to let-7a positions 11–16, with a +4 nt offset, was particularly effective for enhancing site affinity.
source: Each had a contiguous stretch of 6–8 perfect Watson–Crick pairs to the let-7a 3′ region, usually including the ACAACC k-mer, which suggested that perfect pairing to let-7a positions 11–16, with a +4 nt offset, was particularly effective for enhancing site affinity.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the enrichment patterns observed in the data.

claim: Relative KD values corresponding to a broad spectrum of 3′-pairing architectures spanned a several hundred–fold range.
source: Relative KD values corresponding to a broad spectrum of 3′-pairing architectures spanned a several hundred–fold range, with strong agreement observed between the results of replicate experiments performed independently with different preparations of both AGO2–let-7a and the let-7a programmed library (r2 = 0.96, n = 1477; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, left).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Compensatory pairing to miRNA nucleotides 11–16 at optimal offsets yielded binding affinities comparable to that of the canonical 6mer.
source: Nearly all possibilities examined had values readily distinguished from the log-averaged value for seed-mismatched sites alone, with compensatory pairing to miRNA nucleotides 11–16 at optimal offsets yielding binding affinities comparable to that of the canonical 6mer (Figure 2B, left).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Pairing to the GGUUGU segment spanning positions 11–16 of let-7a is the most consequential for 3′-compensatory pairing.
source: Further inspection of longer 3′ sites underscored the conclusion that pairing to the GGUUGU segment spanning positions 11–16 of let-7a is the most consequential for 3′-compensatory pairing, as all optimal pairing positions for 3′ sites ≥6 nt in length paired to this segment.
evidence: This statement is an inference based on the analysis of optimal pairing positions.

claim: Pairing to the 5′ end of the GGUUGU segment (containing the sequence GGUU) was more impactful than pairing to its 3′ end.
source: Moreover, inspection of the optimal positions for shorter sites showed that pairing to the 5′ end of this segment (containing the sequence GGUU) was more impactful than pairing to its 3′ end (Figure 2B, right).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Increasing the length of pairing from 4 to 11 bp led to a shift in the optimal offset, with a preferred offset of +2 nt when pairing with 4 bp compared to a preferred offset of +4 nt when pairing with 9–11 bp.
source: In addition, increasing the length of pairing from 4 to 11 bp led not only to increased binding affinity at almost all offsets, as might have been expected, but also to a shift in the optimal offset, with a preferred offset of +2 nt when pairing with 4 bp compared to a preferred offset of +4 nt when pairing with 9–11 bp (Figure 2B, left).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: For 3′ sites of each length, those that began at let-7a position 12 had intermediate affinity and optimal offsets of 0 or +1 nt, with clearly reduced affinity as offsets increased beyond +1 nt.
source: For 3′ sites of each length, those that began at let-7a position 12 (dark blue points of Figure 2C) had intermediate affinity and optimal offsets of 0 or +1 nt, with clearly reduced affinity as offsets increased beyond +1 nt.
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: At offsets of 0 or +1 nt, 3′ sites that began at position 11 had affinities similar to those that began at position 12, but at more positive offsets, sites beginning at 11 had strikingly increased affinity, with affinity peaking at offsets of +2 or +3 nt.
source: At these offsets of 0 or +1 nt, 3′ sites that began at position 11 (dark purple points) had affinities similar to those that began at position 12. However, in stark contrast to the sites beginning at position 12, sites beginning at 11 had strikingly increased affinity at more positive offsets, with affinity peaking at offsets of +2 or +3 nt.
evidence: This statement is based on data analysis comparing different pairing positions and offsets.

claim: Pairing to position 11 in the central region of the miRNA is less accessible than pairing to position 12, and therefore a longer loop in the target sequence is required to bridge seed pairing with 3′ pairing that includes position 11.
source: These results suggested that pairing to position 11 in the central region of the miRNA is less accessible than pairing to position 12, and therefore a longer loop in the target sequence is required to bridge seed pairing with 3′ pairing that includes position 11 (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed offset preferences for different pairing positions.

claim: When the increased offset enables pairing to position 11, substantially greater affinity can be achieved.
source: Nonetheless, when the increased offset enables pairing to position 11, substantially greater affinity can be achieved.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed affinity patterns.

claim: The positive-offset binding mode includes pairing to miRNA position 11 and greatly benefits from short positive offsets.
source: We call this newly defined binding mode, which includes pairing to miRNA position 11 and greatly benefits from short positive offsets, the 'positive-offset' binding mode.
evidence: This is a definition based on the observed data patterns.

claim: The zero-offset binding mode lacks pairing to position 11 and does not benefit from offsets greater than +1 nt.
source: Accordingly, the more conventional binding mode, which lacks pairing to position 11 and does not benefit from offsets greater than +1 nt, we call the 'zero-offset' binding mode.
evidence: This is a definition based on the observed data patterns.

claim: Some of the weakest relative affinities were observed for extended 3′-pairing possibilities that began at position 9 with an offset of 0 nt, which were attributable to AGO2-catalyzed slicing of molecules with extensive contiguous pairing.
source: Some of the weakest relative affinities were observed for extended 3′-pairing possibilities that began at position 9 with an offset of 0 nt (Figure 2B and C, asterisks). These weak values were attributable to AGO2-catalzyed slicing of molecules with extensive contiguous pairing, which would have depleted these molecules from our bound library.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed weak affinities and knowledge of AGO2 slicing activity.

claim: Pairing to let-7a positions 10–20 at an optimal offset length of +4 nt conferred an ~380-fold increase in affinity over the average seed-mismatched site alone, leading to an overall binding affinity rivaling that of the canonical 8mer.
source: At the optimal offset length of +4 nt, pairing to let-7a positions 10–20 conferred an ~380-fold increase in affinity over the average seed-mismatched site alone (Figure 2E), leading to an overall binding affinity rivaling that of the canonical 8mer (Figure 2B).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figures 2E and 2B.

claim: Previous low-throughput measurements found that pairing to miRNA positions 13–16 of let-7a confers a 1.6–2-fold increase in binding affinity.
source: Previous low-throughput measurements of the benefit of 3′ pairing for let-7a examined the influence of pairing to miRNA positions 13–16 at an offset of 0 nt and found that this pairing confers a 1.6–2-fold increase in binding affinity (Wee et al., 2012; Salomon et al., 2015).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Wee et al., 2012 and Salomon et al., 2015.

claim: The authors' measurements for the 4-nt 3′ site pairing to positions 13–16 of let-7a indicated that it conferred a 1.5-fold increase in affinity.
source: Likewise, our measurements for this 4-nt 3′ site indicated that it conferred a 1.5-fold increase in affinity (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Maintaining the offset of 0 nt and the pairing position of 13 and extending pairing to the very 3′ end of let-7a increased the binding affinity to only 3.1-fold.
source: Furthermore, maintaining the offset of 0 nt and the pairing position of 13 and extending pairing to the very 3′ end of let-7a increased the binding affinity to only 3.1-fold (Figure 2E).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Most of the conclusions regarding binding affinities inferred from AGO-RBNS also held with respect to repression in cells.
source: Most of the conclusions regarding binding affinities inferred from AGO-RBNS also held with respect to repression in cells, including the marginal benefit of pairing to only nucleotides 13–16 of let-7a, the greater benefit of pairing to let-7a nucleotides 11–19 compared to nucleotides 13–21, the strong benefit of a positive offset when pairing to nucleotides 11–19 of let-7a but not when pairing to nucleotides 13–16 or 13–21, and the ability of extended 3′-compensatory pairing at a favorable position and offset to impart activity matching that of the canonical 8mer site (Figure 3B).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 3B from the reporter assay.

claim: Among the sites with pairing to nucleotides 11–19 of let-7a, the most effective was the one with an offset of +4 nt formed by insertion of four consecutive A nucleotides within the segment of the target that linked seed and 3′ pairing.
source: Among the sites with pairing to nucleotides 11–19 of let-7a, the most effective was the one with an offset of +4 nt formed by insertion of four consecutive A nucleotides within the segment of the target that linked seed and 3′ pairing (Figure 3B, +4A).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The +4A site was more effective than the two possibilities with an offset of +1 formed by insertion of either a single A or U nucleotide (+1A and +1U, respectively; p < 0.02, Tukey's range test).
source: This site was more effective than the two possibilities with an offset of +1 formed by insertion of either a single A or U nucleotide (+1A and +1U, respectively; p < 0.02, Tukey's range test), which were in turn more effective than the site that lacked an insertion (0) and thus had a 0-nt offset (Figure 3B, p < 10−4, Tukey's range test).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 3B with statistical testing.

claim: The primary nucleotide identity of the segment that links seed and 3′ pairing can modulate repression.
source: These results indicated that the primary nucleotide identity of the segment that links seed and 3′ pairing can modulate repression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences in efficacy between +4A and +4U sites.

claim: Compared to the single-site configurations, the dual-site configuration yielded greater repression, with an average increase of ~2.8-fold, implying some cooperativity in the action of the two sites.
source: Compared to the single-site configurations, the dual-site configuration yielded greater repression, with an average increase of ~2.8-fold (Figure 3B), implying some cooperativity in the action of the two sites (Grimson et al., 2007; Saetrom et al., 2007; Broderick et al., 2011; Briskin et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 3B and supported by citations.

claim: The most effective synthetic 3′-compensatory sites tested (those with complementarity to nucleotides 11–19 and with a +1A-nt or +4A-nt offset) were more repressive on average than the two sites found within lin-41 mRNA of C. elegans (p < 10−3, 1.2-fold more repressive).
source: The most effective synthetic 3′-compensatory sites tested (those with complementarity to nucleotides 11–19 and with a +1A-nt or +4A-nt offset) were more repressive on average than the two sites found within lin-41 mRNA of C. elegans (p < 10−3, 1.2-fold more repressive).
evidence: This statement is based on data comparison with statistical testing.

claim: Affinity observed in vitro corresponded well to repression observed in cells (r2 = 0.71).
source: Overall, we found that affinity observed in vitro corresponded well to repression observed in cells (Figure 3C, r2 = 0.71).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Stabilizing 3′ pairing was observed for both miR-1 and miR-155, with binding affinity increasing with the length of pairing.
source: Stabilizing 3′ pairing was observed for both miR-1 (Figure 4A) and miR-155 (Figure 4B), with binding affinity increasing with the length of pairing, as observed for let-7a (Figure 2).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: The magnitude of increased binding affinity from 3′ pairing differed between let-7a, miR-1, and miR-155: the affinity of 3′ pairing to miR-1 was more modest, with 3′-compensatory sites seldomly reaching the affinity of its canonical 6mer site.
source: However, the magnitude of increased binding affinity differed from that of let-7a and that of each other: the affinity of 3′ pairing to miR-1 was more modest, with 3′-compensatory sites seldomly reaching the affinity of its canonical 6mer site (Figure 4A), whereas for miR-155, they often reached the affinity of its canonical 8mer site, and in some cases increased affinity by >500-fold (Figure 4B).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: For miR-155, 3′-compensatory sites often reached the affinity of its canonical 8mer site, and in some cases increased affinity by >500-fold.
source: However, the magnitude of increased binding affinity differed from that of let-7a and that of each other: the affinity of 3′ pairing to miR-1 was more modest, with 3′-compensatory sites seldomly reaching the affinity of its canonical 6mer site (Figure 4A), whereas for miR-155, they often reached the affinity of its canonical 8mer site, and in some cases increased affinity by >500-fold (Figure 4B).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: For miR-1, optimal 4-nt sites paired to miRNA nucleotides 12–15, and when considering optimal sites of increasing lengths, pairing extended continuously, primarily toward the 3′ end of the miRNA and never reaching miRNA nucleotide 10.
source: For miR-1, optimal 4-nt sites paired to miRNA nucleotides 12–15, and when considering optimal sites of increasing lengths, pairing extended continuously, primarily toward the 3′ end of the miRNA and never reaching miRNA nucleotide 10 (Figure 4A, right).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For miR-155, optimal 4-nt sites paired to miRNA nucleotides 13–16, and for optimal sites of increasing lengths, pairing sometimes shifted discontinuously and never included miRNA nucleotide 12.
source: By contrast, for miR-155, optimal 4-nt sites paired to miRNA nucleotides 13–16, and for optimal sites of increasing lengths, pairing sometimes shifted discontinuously and never included miRNA nucleotide 12 (Figure 4B, right).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Unlike sites for let-7a, those for neither miR-1 nor miR-155 underwent a significant shift in the preferred offset.
source: Analysis of each of the optimal 3′ sites of miR-1 and miR-155 along the length of the random region indicated that, unlike sites for let-7a, those for neither of these two miRNAs underwent a significant shift in the preferred offset (Figure 4A and B, left).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: The longer optimal sites of miR-1 extended to position 11, and their range of near-optimal offsets broadened to include values from 0 to +5 nt, consistent with contributions from both binding modes.
source: Nevertheless, the longer optimal sites of miR-1 extended to position 11, and their range of near-optimal offsets broadened to include values from 0 to +5 nt, consistent with contributions from both binding modes.
evidence: This statement is based on data analysis and inference about binding modes.

claim: The offset preferences of miR-155 broadened with increased pairing, coinciding with pairing to the G19-G20-G21-G22 stretch near the 3′ end of miR-155.
source: The offset preferences of miR-155 also broadened with increased pairing. However, instead of coinciding with pairing at position 11, these broadened preferences coincided with pairing to the G19-G20-G21-G22 stretch near the 3′ end of miR-155.
evidence: This statement is based on data analysis.

claim: The most optimal 3′ sites each paired to at least two nucleotides of the miRNA segment spanning positions 13–16, which was previously identified as most consequential for 3′ pairing, but frequently did not pair to the entire segment.
source: In summary, the most optimal 3′ sites each paired to at least two nucleotides of the miRNA segment spanning positions 13–16, which was previously identified as most consequential for 3′ pairing, but frequently did not pair to the entire segment.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on data analysis across multiple miRNAs.

claim: Shorter optimal sites consistently preferred pairing to G nucleotides adjacent to miRNA positions 13–16.
source: Shorter optimal sites consistently preferred pairing to G nucleotides adjacent to miRNA positions 13–16.
evidence: This is a summary statement based on data analysis across multiple miRNAs.

claim: Association of the guide RNA with the AGO protein does not fully standardize either the architecture of optimal 3′ pairing or the magnitude of its benefit.
source: Thus, our results indicated that association of the guide RNA with the AGO protein does not fully standardize either the architecture of optimal 3′ pairing or the magnitude of its benefit.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed differences between miRNAs.

claim: The effect of pairing offset was largely independent of the effect of guide–target complementarity for each of the three miRNAs.
source: The similarities observed between heat maps for the same miRNA at different offsets indicated that each change in offset altered the binding affinity of all 3′-pairing possibilities in a consistent manner, which in turn indicated that for each of the three miRNAs, the effect of pairing offset was largely independent of the effect of guide–target complementarity (Figures 2E and 4C, D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns in the heat maps.

claim: A multiplicative model of pairing and offset coefficients fit the data well (r2 = 0.92, 0.86, and 0.96 for let-7a, miR-1, and miR-155, respectively).
source: Our model fit the data well (r2 = 0.92, 0.86, and 0.96 for let-7a, miR-1, and miR-155, respectively; Figure 5—figure supplement 1), and yielded a set of pairing and offset coefficients for each miRNA.
evidence: This statement is based on model fitting to the data.

claim: Compared to RNA free in solution, association with AGO reduces the differences in binding energy observed when hybridizing to different miRNA 3′-end sequences.
source: Thus, as observed with the miRNA seed region (Salomon et al., 2015; McGeary et al., 2019), compared to RNA free in solution, association with AGO reduces the differences in binding energy observed when hybridizing to different miRNA 3′-end sequences.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of observed affinities with predicted thermodynamic values, supported by citations.

claim: The benefit of pairing to 3′ sites was mostly offset by the cost of disrupting favorable interactions between unpaired 3′ regions and AGO.
source: Presumably, the benefit of pairing to 3′ sites was mostly offset by the cost of disrupting favorable interactions between unpaired 3′ regions and AGO, as proposed in the context of fully paired sites (Tomari and Zamore, 2005).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed reduction in binding energy benefit, supported by citation.

claim: The magnitude of the inferred cost of disrupting AGO-miRNA interactions appeared specific to each miRNA, implying that AGO might have some sequence preferences when interacting with unpaired miRNA 3′ regions.
source: The magnitude of this inferred cost appeared specific to each miRNA, implying that AGO might have some sequence preferences when interacting with unpaired miRNA 3′ regions.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed differences between miRNAs.

claim: Separating the comparison between KD fold-change and predicted ∆G based on whether the contiguous range of pairing included the G11, G12, and G20 of let-7a, miR-1, and miR-155, respectively, revealed a cooperative benefit of pairing to these nucleotides.
source: Separating the comparison between KD fold-change and predicted ∆G based on whether the contiguous range of pairing included the G11, G12, and G20 of let-7a, miR-1, and miR-155, respectively, revealed a cooperative benefit of pairing to these nucleotides (Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C), such that their inclusion within the 3′ pairing enabled the other paired nucleotides to contribute more to the interaction.
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2B, C.

claim: The added affinity of a 3′ site was relatively constant when it supplemented different sites that had seed matches.
source: The added affinity of a 3′ site was relatively constant when it supplemented different sites that had seed matches (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 8), whereas it varied in the context of different 3′-compensatory sites that had different seed mismatches (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplements 5–7).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figures 5H, 5F, and supplementary figures.

claim: The added affinity of a 3′ site varied in the context of different 3′-compensatory sites that had different seed mismatches.
source: The added affinity of a 3′ site was relatively constant when it supplemented different sites that had seed matches (Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 8), whereas it varied in the context of different 3′-compensatory sites that had different seed mismatches (Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplements 5–7).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figures 5F and supplementary figures.

claim: The effects of seed mismatches were miRNA-specific and unrelated to their binding affinities.
source: The effects of seed mismatches were miRNA-specific and unrelated to their binding affinities (Figure 5G).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Experiments using chimeric miRNAs demonstrated the separability of the mismatch effects from the length, position, offset, and nucleotide-identity preferences of the 3′ region.
source: Additionally, our experiments using chimeric miRNAs demonstrated the separability of the mismatch effects from the length, position, offset, and nucleotide-identity preferences of the 3′ region (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Both the pairing and offset preferences tracked with the 3′ sequence in chimeric miRNAs.
source: Results for these variants showed that both the pairing and offset preferences tracked with the 3′ sequence (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–G), with the quantitative contribution of each 3′ nucleotide to pairing largely maintained when shifted to an adjacent position (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–E).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: The seed-mismatch preferences tracked with the seed sequence in chimeric miRNAs.
source: By contrast, the seed-mismatch preferences tracked with the seed sequence, with little pairwise difference in these preferences observed for miRNA variants sharing nucleotides 1–8 but possessing distinct 3′ sequences (Figure 6—figure supplement 1H, I and Figure 6—figure supplement 2F).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 6—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: No imperfections (mismatches, wobbles, or bulges) increased 3′-site affinity, indicating that there were no positions at which the altered helical geometry of a mismatch was favored over Watson–Crick pairing.
source: Analysis of these variants in the context of the best sites at each length (Figure 7A–C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1) revealed no imperfections that increased 3′-site affinity, which indicated that there were no positions at which the altered helical geometry of a mismatch was favored over Watson–Crick pairing.
evidence: This is an inference based on data shown in Figures 7A–C and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Larger effects of mismatches were observed for mismatches involving any of nucleotides 11–15 of let-7a, 12–15 of miR-1, and 15–22 of miR-155, which concurred with the importance of extending pairing to G11-G12, G12, and G19-G20-G21-G22 of the respective miRNAs.
source: Nonetheless, effects at some positions were more striking than others, with larger effects observed for mismatches involving any of nucleotides 11–15 of let-7a (Figure 7A), 12–15 of miR-1 (Figure 7B), and 15–22 of miR-155 (Figure 7C), which concurred with the importance of extending pairing to G11-G12, G12, and G19-G20-G21-G22 of the respective miRNAs.
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figures 7A–C.

claim: The effect of a mismatch to a particular nucleotide was informed primarily by the overall importance of that miRNA nucleotide for pairing (as determined by its nucleotide identity and position within the miRNA 3′ end), irrespective of whether the target nucleotide fell within the middle or terminus of the 3′ site.
source: Thus, in some nearest-neighbor and positional contexts, pairing to a miRNA C nucleotide can be as important as pairing to a miRNA G nucleotide. More generally, these results showed that the effect of a mismatch to a particular nucleotide was informed primarily by the overall importance of that miRNA nucleotide for pairing (as determined by its nucleotide identity and position within the miRNA 3′ end), irrespective of whether the target nucleotide fell within the middle or terminus of the 3′ site.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of mismatch effects across different positions.

claim: At each position, the severity of both deletions and bulges tracked with that observed for the mismatches, with the effects of deletions generally similar to those of their corresponding mismatches, and effects of bulged nucleotides marginally less severe.
source: At each position, the severity of both types of lesions tracked with that observed for the mismatches, with the effects of deletions generally similar to those of their corresponding mismatches, and effects of bulged nucleotides marginally less severe.
evidence: This is a summary of the observed patterns in the data.

claim: A small but significant benefit to terminal bulges was observed for each miRNA (p = 2.4 × 10−5, 1.4 × 10−6, and 4.5 × 10−4 for let-7a, miR-1, and miR-155, respectively; one-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test).
source: For each miRNA, a small but significant benefit to terminal bulges was observed (Figure 7F; p = 2.4 × 10−5, 1.4 × 10−6, and 4.5 × 10−4 for let-7a, miR-1, and miR-155, respectively; one-tailed Wilcoxon signed rank test).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 7F with statistical testing.

claim: The effects of mismatches within 3′ pairing were typically much lower than expected for RNA in solution, with no strong relationship between the observed and predicted ∆∆G values (r2 = 0.02).
source: Comparison of these values with those predicted using the nearest-neighbor parameters revealed that the effects of the mismatches were typically much lower than expected for RNA in solution, with no strong relationship between the observed and predicted ∆∆G values (Figure 7G, left; r2 = 0.02).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: The miRNA–target U:G wobble was as disruptive as the typical mismatch but predicted to be much less so.
source: The outlier in this analysis was the miRNA–target U:G wobble, which was as disruptive as the typical mismatch but predicted to be much less so (Figure 7G, left, green +).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: For eight of 12 mismatches, the fractional reduction in ∆G was within 10% of its prediction, but the miRNA–target A:G, G:G, G:U, and U:G mismatches respectively caused 31%, 42%, 21%, and 48% more reduction in binding energy than predicted.
source: For eight of 12 mismatches, the fractional reduction in ∆G was within 10% of its prediction, but the miRNA–target A:G, G:G, G:U, and U:G mismatches respectively caused 31%, 42%, 21%, and 48% more reduction in binding energy than predicted.
evidence: This statement is based on data analysis comparing observed and predicted values.

claim: The nearest-neighbor parameters were not suited for predicting the contribution of miRNA 3′ pairing in three respects: (1) the overall contribution to binding energy was far less than that predicted, (2) mismatched target G nucleotides were relatively more deleterious than predicted, and (3) wobble pairing was relatively less favorable than predicted.
source: These results indicated that the nearest-neighbor parameters were not suited for predicting the contribution of miRNA 3′ pairing in three respects: (1) the overall contribution to binding energy was far less than that predicted, (2) mismatched target G nucleotides were relatively more deleterious than predicted, and (3) wobble pairing was relatively less favorable than predicted.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of observed and predicted values.

claim: A mismatch within the seed pairing had a much larger influence on ∆∆G than did a mismatch within the 3′ pairing.
source: These analyses indicated that the effects of mismatches within seed pairing also did not agree with predicted pairing energetics, albeit differently than the effects of mismatches within 3′ pairing. First, a mismatch within the seed pairing had a much larger influence on ∆∆G than did a mismatch within the 3′ pairing.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of mismatch effects in seed vs. 3′ pairing.

claim: The reductions in binding affinities for mismatches within the seed pairing were even more regular than those for mismatches within the 3′ pairing, with a ~3 kcal/mol detriment for each of the 12 mismatch/wobble possibilities.
source: Moreover, the reductions in binding affinities for mismatches within the seed pairing were even more regular than those for mismatches within the 3′ pairing, with a ~3 kcal/mol detriment for each of the 12 mismatch/wobble possibilities (Figure 7H, left).
evidence: This statement is based on data shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The binding preferences at both the seed and 3′ regions of the miRNA were not well explained by nearest-neighbor rules, although the nature of the deviations differed in these two regions.
source: Thus, the binding preferences at both the seed and 3′ regions of the miRNA were not well explained by nearest-neighbor rules, although the nature of the deviations differed in these two regions.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of mismatch effects in both regions.

claim: Productive 3′ pairing can encompass the entire miRNA 3′ region and should not be thought of as limited to a short 3′-supplementary region.
source: Thus, productive 3′ pairing can encompass the entire miRNA 3′ region and should not be thought of as limited to a short 3′-supplementary region.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed data showing that 3′-site affinities nearly always increased as potential for pairing expanded.

claim: The preferred positions of 3′ pairing can vary widely between miRNAs, to include virtually any nucleotide downstream of the seed.
source: These observations showing that the preferred positions of 3′ pairing can vary so widely between miRNAs, to include virtually any nucleotide downstream of the seed, argued strongly against assigning the same short 3′-supplementary region to all miRNAs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed differences in optimal pairing positions between miRNAs.

claim: The observations that pairing to nucleotides 11–14 of let-7a imparted greater affinity than did pairing to nucleotides 13–16 and that pairing to nucleotides 11–19 imparted greater repression than did pairing to nucleotides 13–21 concurred with recent analyses of the relative importance of these nucleotides in Caenorhabditis elegans.
source: Our observations that pairing to nucleotides 11–14 of let-7a imparted greater affinity than did pairing to nucleotides 13–16 (Figure 2B and C) and that pairing to nucleotides 11–19 imparted greater repression than did pairing to nucleotides 13–21 (Figure 3), concurred with recent analyses of the relative importance of these nucleotides in Caenorhabditis elegans.
evidence: This statement connects the study's findings to previous work in C. elegans.

claim: C. elegans requires let-7 repression of lin-41 for viability, and this repression occurs through two 3′-compensatory sites that each have pairing to nucleotides 11–19 of the miRNA.
source: C. elegans requires let-7 repression of lin-41 for viability, and this repression occurs through two 3′-compensatory sites that each have pairing to nucleotides 11–19 of the miRNA (Figure 3A; Pasquinelli et al., 2000; Reinhart et al., 2000; Aeschimann et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Pasquinelli et al., 2000, Reinhart et al., 2000, and Aeschimann et al., 2019.

claim: Mutagenesis of individual nucleotides of the let-7 miRNA indicates that nucleotides 11, 12, and 13 are each critical for viability in C. elegans, whereas nucleotides 14, 15, and 16 each have intermediate importance, and nucleotides 17, 18, and 19 each have no detectable importance.
source: Mutagenesis of individual nucleotides of the let-7 miRNA indicates that nucleotides 11, 12, and 13 are each critical for viability, whereas nucleotides 14, 15, and 16 each have intermediate importance, and nucleotides 17, 18, and 19 each have no detectable importance (Duan et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Duan et al., 2021.

claim: The crystal structure of AGO2–miR-122 bound to a 3′-supplementary target shows that miRNA nucleotides 9–11 are not available for pairing due to both helical distortion and inaccessibility caused by residues of the PIWI and L2 loop.
source: The structure of AGO2–miR-122 bound to a 3′-supplementary site, which shows that miRNA nucleotides 9–11 are not available for pairing due to both helical distortion and inaccessibility caused by residues of the PIWI and L2 loop, seems to support the notion of a 3′-supplementary region at nucleotides 13–16 (Sheu-Gruttadauria et al., 2019b).
evidence: This statement is supported by citation to Sheu-Gruttadauria et al., 2019b.

claim: The structure of AGO2–miR-122 bound to a 3′-supplementary target reflects the conformation of the zero-offset binding mode.
source: We suggest that this structure reflects the conformation of the zero-offset binding mode, as it provides a physical model for why extension of potential pairing from nucleotide 12 to nucleotide 11 results in almost no increased binding affinity (Figure 5—figure supplement 4) for sites with an offset of 0 nt.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural data and the observed binding affinities.

claim: The two 3′-binding modes both appear to be compatible with either of the two gene-regulatory processes that involve 3′ pairing—TDMD and miRNA-mediated repression.
source: Thus, the two 3′-binding modes both appear to be compatible with either of the two gene-regulatory processes that involve 3′ pairing—TDMD and miRNA-mediated repression.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that both binding modes are represented in known TDMD and repression examples.
